exemplarHeadings: A cold hand gives us a starting point

records.actualTextRead: A flower colour disappears, then returns Mendel crossed pea plants from lines with purple flowers and lines with white flowers. The first offspring generation had purple flowers. The colours had not produced the pale-purple blend that a blending explanation would suggest. When that generation reproduced, white flowers appeared again. How could a phenotype disappear for a generation without its allele being lost? Keep the distinction from lesson01 in view. A {{v:phenotype|phenotype}} is an expressed characteristic, such as flower colour. A {{v:genotype|genotype}} is the allele combination at the locus being considered. An {{v:allele|allele}} is a version of a gene, and a locus is the gene's position on a chromosome. An allele can be present in the genotype even when its associated recessive phenotype is not expressed.

nativePassageBindings.text: A gene is a DNA sequence associated with a functional product or characteristic. Alternative versions are alleles. In a diploid autosomal model, an individual inherits one allele from each parent and therefore has two alleles at the locus being studied.

The genotype is the allele combination, such as BB, Bb or bb. The phenotype is the observed or measured characteristic, such as dark or pale pigment. A phenotype can also be an enzyme activity or another physiological property, not only a visible feature.

Suppose a stated model says B gives dark pigment and is completely dominant to b. BB and Bb individuals have the dark phenotype, while bb individuals have the pale phenotype. The same phenotype can therefore correspond to more than one genotype.

exactExemplarPassageBindings.heading: A cold hand gives us a starting point
exactExemplarPassageBindings.uniqueTeachingFunction: A concrete bodily change establishes the chapter question, then the information-flow visual distinguishes jobs and explains why input precedes processing and output.
exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: A cold hand gives us a starting point You step outside without gloves. Your skin cools. A moment later, you pull your hands into your sleeves. Your body has detected a change, processed information about it, and produced a response. This chapter explains how those three jobs happen, from the whole nervous system down to the membrane of a single cell. Start with this question: How can a change at one place in your body produce a useful response somewhere else? We will first follow the information, then examine the cells carrying it, and finally return to the brain and the systems they form. Sensory inputInformation comes in from receptors. → Brain or spinal cord · CNSIntegrationInformation is processed. → Motor outputInstructions go out to effectors. Follow the arrows from sensory input to integration to motor output. The arrows show information flow; the dashed boundary locates processing in the CNS. The boxes describe jobs, not three individual cells. Look at the middle box first. Integration means processing incoming information and organizing a response. The system cannot choose an appropriate response from an outgoing signal alone: information must first arrive. That is why sensory input comes before integration and motor output follows it.

records.actualTextRead: Know what was crossed A {{v:true-breeding|true-breeding}} line consistently produces the same form of the relevant trait when bred within the line under the stated conditions. That description comes from breeding history, not from looking at one plant. In the simple one-gene model used here, the contrasting true-breeding lines are homozygous: each individual has two copies of the same allele at that locus. Controlled crossing makes the parentage known. A pea flower can supply pollen and can also contain eggs. Pollination transfers pollen to the receiving flower; a sperm cell delivered through the pollen tube can later join an egg. That joining is fertilisation . To compare chosen lines, Mendel controlled which plant supplied the pollen instead of allowing an unintended pollen donor or self-pollination to change the cross. The chosen starting parents form the P generation . Their offspring form the {{v:f1-generation|F1 generation}}, the first filial generation. Offspring produced when the F1 plants reproduce in the specified design form the {{v:f2-generation|F2 generation}}. These labels tell you how the generations are related. They do not mean that every P individual is homozygous or every F1 individual is heterozygous in every possible experiment.

nativePassageBindings.text: Homozygous means the two alleles are the same, as in BB or bb. Heterozygous means they differ, as in Bb. A dominant allele is expressed in the heterozygote under the stated complete-dominance model. Dominant does not mean most common, healthiest or strongest.

Mendel studied traits in pea plants and used controlled crosses between lines with contrasting forms. In a simple example, let R represent round seeds and r wrinkled seeds, with complete dominance of R. A true-breeding RR line crossed with rr produces Rr offspring in the F1 generation.

exactExemplarPassageBindings.heading: How can one cell reach a distant muscle?
exactExemplarPassageBindings.uniqueTeachingFunction: A distance problem makes morphology necessary; figure reading establishes one continuous axon, receiving branches and sending terminals before structure–function inference.
exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: How can one cell reach a distant muscle? A nerve signal may need to travel from your spinal cord toward a muscle in your foot. A chain of round, identical cells would not explain the long fibres inside a nerve. Neurons have specialized shapes that let one cell receive many inputs and send information over a considerable distance. Start with a typical multipolar neuron: it has many dendrites and one axon. Dendrites are branching receiving regions. The cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and organelles and maintains the cell's metabolism. The axon carries action potentials toward its terminal branches. An action potential is a brief electrical change across a neuron’s membrane. Regenerating that change along the axon carries a nerve signal. For now, connect this signal with the continuous axon; Lessons 4 and 5 will explain the ion movements that produce it. An axon terminal passes a signal to another cell at a junction called a synapse. Read from dendrites to axon terminals. This is a simplified illustration of a typical multipolar neuron, not every neuron shape. Look first at the large yellow cell body on the left. Trace one short branch outward: that is a dendrite. Now follow the long yellow extension to the right under the blue coverings. That continuous extension is the axon; the blue coverings are insulation around it, not separate neurons. The large horizontal arrow means the usual direction of information flow through this model. The narrowed region where the axon begins is labelled the axon hillock. Signals arriving at different receiving regions can combine and influence whether an action potential begins near the start of the axon. The cell body does not consciously choose. Its membranes respond to the combined electrical effects of incoming signals. Finish at the terminal branches. Their branching allows the neuron to communicate with more than one target. The next cell is separated from a chemical synaptic terminal by a tiny synaptic cleft. The electrical signal along an axon and the chemical signal across that cleft are different parts of the pathway.

exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: Use structure to explain function Question: Why does a neuron benefit from having many short dendritic branches and one long axon? A useful answer must explain what the shape makes possible. Begin with reception. Many dendritic branches provide a large receiving surface. This allows many synaptic contacts rather than just one input.Connect reception to integration. Inputs influence the cell body and the region where the axon begins. Combining those effects allows the outgoing signal to depend on more than one incoming message.Connect length to distance. records.actualTextRead: Each parent contributes one allele A chromosome is a DNA-bearing structure carrying many genes. In an ordinary diploid cell there are two chromosome sets. The corresponding chromosomes form a homologous pair : one came from each parent, and both carry the same kinds of genes at corresponding loci. An Rr individual has R at the seed-shape locus on one homologue and r at that locus on the other. Before meiosis, DNA is copied. Each chromosome then consists of two sister chromatids , the copied versions joined together. Copying an R-bearing chromosome produces two R-bearing sister copies; it does not turn r into R or mix the two allele versions. We are following ordinary copying and separation, without a mutation changing the allele. Meiosis reduces the chromosome sets from two to one. The homologous chromosomes separate in the first division. The sister chromatids separate in the second division, with no further DNA copying between those divisions. A cell with one chromosome set is haploid . In a flowering plant, the reproductive life cycle produces haploid gametes after this reduction. We only need to follow the allele contribution here: an egg or sperm carries one allele at this locus, not the parent's whole pair. Thus an RR parent can contribute R; an rr parent can contribute r; and an Rr parent can contribute R or r. A {{v:probability|probability}} is the chance of an outcome under the stated conditions. Under ordinary segregation, either allele from the heterozygote has a probability of one half of being in a gamete. Dominance does not decide which chromosome separates into that gamete. The two allele versions remain distinct as they are passed on.

An Rr individual forms gametes containing R or r. The alleles segregate as homologous chromosomes separate during meiosis. In the simple model, each allele has a one-half chance of entering a gamete.

records.actualTextRead: From the starting cross to the second generation Start with the true-breeding seed-shape lines: RR × rr . The multiplication-style cross sign means these are the two parents being crossed; it is not an instruction to multiply the letters. The RR parent contributes R in its gametes. The rr parent contributes r. At fertilisation, one egg and one sperm join, restoring a pair of alleles in the zygote , the first cell of the offspring. Every combination available in this cross is therefore Rr. Applying the phenotype rule after combining the alleles gives round F1 seeds. The r allele is still present in each seed's genotype. Grow the F1 seeds into plants. When an Rr F1 plant self-pollinates, its eggs can carry R or r and its sperm can carry R or r. The same allele-combination reasoning applies to a controlled cross between two Rr F1 plants. The F2 cross is Rr × Rr . Read the small grid from its edges inward. The left edge gives an egg's allele; the top edge gives a sperm's allele. Each interior entry combines those two contributions. The edges represent gamete possibilities, and the interior entries represent offspring genotypes. They are not the same kind of cell. Possible F2 allele combinations from Rr × Rr Egg allele ↓ / sperm allele → R, probability ½ r, probability ½ R, probability ½ RR — round Rr — round r, probability ½ rR — round rr — wrinkled Follow the lower-right entry first. The egg contributes r and the sperm contributes r, so the offspring is rr and expresses the wrinkled phenotype. Neither allele had to be recreated. Both were available in the F1 parents before they formed gametes. Now compare the upper-right and lower-left entries. Rr and rR are the same heterozygous genotype; the written order only shows which gamete supplied which allele in this table. The gene in this model is autosomal , meaning it is on a chromosome other than a sex chromosome. Here the complete-dominance rule is the same whichever parent supplied R. With equal R/r gamete probabilities and random fertilisation, the four contribution pairs are equally likely. They group into 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr for genotype. RR and Rr both express round seeds, so the phenotype grouping is 3 round : 1 wrinkled . Grouping by appearance combines two genotype categories; it does not change the allele pairs inside them. This distinction separates two processes. Segregation produces single-allele contributions as homologous chromosomes separate during gamete production. Random fertilisation combines one parent's gamete with the other's. Chromosomes aligning in one parent's meiosis do not themselves join that parent's gamete to a gamete from another parent.

exactExemplarPassageBindings.heading: Worked model: include inhibition in the calculation
exactExemplarPassageBindings.uniqueTeachingFunction: Combines signed contributions, applies a net change to a starting voltage, compares with threshold, then changes inhibition while limiting what the simplified model claims.
exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: Worked model: include inhibition in the calculationUse a simplified additive model at the trigger region. Resting voltage is −70 mV, threshold is −55 mV, and simultaneous contributions are +8 mV, +9 mV, and −5 mV.Add all contributions. +8 + 9 − 5 = +12 mV. Leaving out the inhibitory term would overestimate the net depolarization.Apply the net change to the starting value. −70 + 12 = −58 mV.Compare with threshold. −58 is still below −55, so no action potential is initiated in this model.Test the changed condition. exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: A cold hand gives us a starting point You step outside without gloves. Your skin cools. A moment later, you pull your hands into your sleeves. Your body has detected a change, processed information about it, and produced a response. This chapter explains how those three jobs happen, from the whole nervous system down to the membrane of a single cell. Start with this question: How can a change at one place in your body produce a useful response somewhere else? We will first follow the information, then examine the cells carrying it, and finally return to the brain and the systems they form. Sensory inputInformation comes in from receptors. → Brain or spinal cord · CNSIntegrationInformation is processed. → Motor outputInstructions go out to effectors. Follow the arrows from sensory input to integration to motor output. The arrows show information flow; the dashed boundary locates processing in the CNS. The boxes describe jobs, not three individual cells. Look at the middle box first. Integration means processing incoming information and organizing a response. The system cannot choose an appropriate response from an outgoing signal alone: information must first arrive. That is why sensory input comes before integration and motor output follows it.

exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: How can one cell reach a distant muscle? A nerve signal may need to travel from your spinal cord toward a muscle in your foot. A chain of round, identical cells would not explain the long fibres inside a nerve. Neurons have specialized shapes that let one cell receive many inputs and send information over a considerable distance. Start with a typical multipolar neuron: it has many dendrites and one axon. Dendrites are branching receiving regions. The cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and organelles and maintains the cell's metabolism. The axon carries action potentials toward its terminal branches. An action potential is a brief electrical change across a neuron’s membrane. Regenerating that change along the axon carries a nerve signal. For now, connect this signal with the continuous axon; Lessons 4 and 5 will explain the ion movements that produce it. An axon terminal passes a signal to another cell at a junction called a synapse. Read from dendrites to axon terminals. This is a simplified illustration of a typical multipolar neuron, not every neuron shape. Look first at the large yellow cell body on the left. Trace one short branch outward: that is a dendrite. Now follow the long yellow extension to the right under the blue coverings. That continuous extension is the axon; the blue coverings are insulation around it, not separate neurons. The large horizontal arrow means the usual direction of information flow through this model. The narrowed region where the axon begins is labelled the axon hillock. Signals arriving at different receiving regions can combine and influence whether an action potential begins near the start of the axon. The cell body does not consciously choose. Its membranes respond to the combined electrical effects of incoming signals. Finish at the terminal branches. Their branching allows the neuron to communicate with more than one target. The next cell is separated from a chemical synaptic terminal by a tiny synaptic cleft. The electrical signal along an axon and the chemical signal across that cleft are different parts of the pathway.

exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: How can one cell reach a distant muscle? A nerve signal may need to travel from your spinal cord toward a muscle in your foot. A chain of round, identical cells would not explain the long fibres inside a nerve. Neurons have specialized shapes that let one cell receive many inputs and send information over a considerable distance. Start with a typical multipolar neuron: it has many dendrites and one axon. Dendrites are branching receiving regions. The cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and organelles and maintains the cell's metabolism. The axon carries action potentials toward its terminal branches. An action potential is a brief electrical change across a neuron’s membrane. Regenerating that change along the axon carries a nerve signal. For now, connect this signal with the continuous axon; Lessons 4 and 5 will explain the ion movements that produce it. An axon terminal passes a signal to another cell at a junction called a synapse. Read from dendrites to axon terminals. This is a simplified illustration of a typical multipolar neuron, not every neuron shape. Look first at the large yellow cell body on the left. Trace one short branch outward: that is a dendrite. Now follow the long yellow extension to the right under the blue coverings. That continuous extension is the axon; the blue coverings are insulation around it, not separate neurons. The large horizontal arrow means the usual direction of information flow through this model. The narrowed region where the axon begins is labelled the axon hillock. Signals arriving at different receiving regions can combine and influence whether an action potential begins near the start of the axon. The cell body does not consciously choose. Its membranes respond to the combined electrical effects of incoming signals. Finish at the terminal branches. Their branching allows the neuron to communicate with more than one target. The next cell is separated from a chemical synaptic terminal by a tiny synaptic cleft. The electrical signal along an axon and the chemical signal across that cleft are different parts of the pathway.

records.actualTextRead: Interpret an expected count among 80 plants Suppose 80 seeds from this cross are grown into plants whose fruit can be scored. Treat these as 80 offspring from the same parental model, with no selective loss of a genotype before scoring. An expected count is the predicted average number for a group of that size under the probability model. As in lesson03, calculate it by multiplying the total offspring count by the probability of the requested outcome. For white fruit, include both possible shapes. The white/disk and white/spherical categories cannot describe the same plant in this model, so add their probabilities: ¼ + ¼ = ½. The expected count is 80 × ½ = 40 white-fruit plants . For yellow, spherical fruit, both conditions must hold; only wwdd qualifies. Its probability is ¼, giving 80 × ¼ = 20 yellow, spherical-fruit plants . As a check, each of the four phenotype groups has an expected count of 80 × ¼ = 20, and their expected counts sum to 80. The 40 white-fruit plants combine two of those groups; do not add that overlapping total to the four groups again. These are expectations for the plants grown and scored, not guarantees about germination or exact numbers in one planting. Also distinguish the two directions of reasoning: the observed offspring established what parental alleles were present; the resulting model predicts probabilities for further offspring.

L is completely dominant for smooth leaves; ll gives lobed leaves. The loci assort independently, the stated parentage is known, and these genotype-to-phenotype rules apply reliably. A breeding record with incomplete parental genotypes Record Flower and leaf phenotype What is already known about the genotype Parent 1 Violet flowers, lobed leaves V_ll Parent 2 White flowers, smooth leaves vvL_ One observed offspring White flowers, smooth leaves Use the phenotype rules to determine what is forced and what remains possible. Identify the allele each parent had to contribute to this offspring, state which parental genotype is now forced and which possibilities remain for the other parent, and name a further offspring leaf phenotype that would settle the remaining blank. Explain whether a finite run of smooth-leaf offspring alone would settle it. This practice is optional and ungraded. Save your first explanation, then intentionally open the comparison. A further lobed-leaf offspring would be ll. Parent 1 supplies l, so the second l would have to come from parent 2, forcing that parent to be vvLl. If parent 2 is vvLL, it contributes L every time and all offspring are smooth. If it is vvLl, its L and l contributions make both smooth and lobed offspring possible. You do not need to assign a probability to the two possible parents to state this limit. exactExemplarPassageBindings.actualTextRead: How can one cell reach a distant muscle? A nerve signal may need to travel from your spinal cord toward a muscle in your foot. A chain of round, identical cells would not explain the long fibres inside a nerve. Neurons have specialized shapes that let one cell receive many inputs and send information over a considerable distance. Start with a typical multipolar neuron: it has many dendrites and one axon. Dendrites are branching receiving regions. The cell body, or soma, contains the nucleus and organelles and maintains the cell's metabolism. The axon carries action potentials toward its terminal branches. An action potential is a brief electrical change across a neuron’s membrane. Regenerating that change along the axon carries a nerve signal. For now, connect this signal with the continuous axon; Lessons 4 and 5 will explain the ion movements that produce it. An axon terminal passes a signal to another cell at a junction called a synapse. Read from dendrites to axon terminals. This is a simplified illustration of a typical multipolar neuron, not every neuron shape. Look first at the large yellow cell body on the left. Trace one short branch outward: that is a dendrite. Now follow the long yellow extension to the right under the blue coverings. That continuous extension is the axon; the blue coverings are insulation around it, not separate neurons. The large horizontal arrow means the usual direction of information flow through this model. The narrowed region where the axon begins is labelled the axon hillock. Signals arriving at different receiving regions can combine and influence whether an action potential begins near the start of the axon. The cell body does not consciously choose. Its membranes respond to the combined electrical effects of incoming signals. Finish at the terminal branches. Their branching allows the neuron to communicate with more than one target. The next cell is separated from a chemical synaptic terminal by a tiny synaptic cleft. The electrical signal along an axon and the chemical signal across that cleft are different parts of the pathway.
